items.description:

When it comes to celebrity musicians, we all know about the wild parties, outrageous lifestyles, and legendary stories, but what about their favorite meals and recipes? From comfort foods tied to their cultural heritage to surprisingly luxurious dishes only celebrities can afford, the meals these stars love can reveal a lot  more
items.why_watch: It's a small but genuinely humanizing angle on celebrity culture: not the excess, but the beans-on-toast or childhood stew they actually craved. Weird History Food tends to dig up specific, sourced details rather than recycling the same Elvis-peanut-butter anecdotes. If you've ever wondered what Tina Turner or Freddie Mercury actually ate on an ordinary Tuesday, this delivers that quietly satisfying answer.

items.title: 3,000 Meters Down: What NOAA Found in the Deep Ocean
items.description:
More than 3,000 meters beneath the surface, NOAA researchers explored the deep seafloor during the 2023 Alaska expedition. Along the way, they encountered strange deep-sea creatures, sponges, sea pens, and other life in the darkness. This is Dive 1 of their expedition.

Footage: NOAA Ocean Exploration. Independently edited and produced; not affiliated with or endorsed by NOAA.

#deepsea  #deepoceanlife  #oceanexploration  #deepseacreature  #marinelife  #noaa  #alaska  #deepseaexploration
items.why_watch: This is edited-down footage from NOAA's real 2023 Alaska deep-sea expedition, giving you a front-row seat to a seafloor most marine biologists will never visit in person. The 3,000-meter depth means the creatures on screen — sponges, sea pens, whatever else drifts into frame — are genuinely rarely documented. It's less a produced documentary and more a quiet, almost meditative window into a world that exists completely indifferent to ours.

discovery_articles.title: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope Launches to Find Exoplanets and Unravel Mysteries of Dark Matter and Dark Energy
discovery_articles.snippet: The new observatory will complete three surveys of the universe in five years, although it's designed to function at least twice as long. Its data could change scientists' basic understanding of the cosmos
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Named for NASA's first Chief of Astronomy — a woman who fought bureaucratic indifference in the 1960s to make the Hubble Space Telescope possible — Roman's namesake observatory may now rewrite the very physics she spent her career advancing. There's something quietly poetic about a telescope bearing her name being tasked with unraveling mysteries the universe has kept since before humans existed.

garden_note.note: Late August in Zürich carries that particular golden-hour melancholy — the light is still generous but the shadows are stretching longer, and the dahlias seem to know it, blazing all the harder for it. Step outside before the dew settles and listen: the garden is beginning its quiet negotiation with September.
